meta.title: Who really said "Do You Want Six or Eight Slices of Pizza?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not George Carlin's. The six-or-eight pizza gag ran unsigned in U.S. newspapers in June 1965; Parade tied it to Carlin only in 1968, as a favorite joke.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do You Want Six or Eight Slices of Pizza?'?
meta.ogDescription: Unsigned newspaper filler in June 1965, pinned to several different tellers, then to Carlin in 1968 and Yogi Berra by 1970. No proven author.

answer.label: Not George Carlin — an anonymous 1965 newspaper gag
answer.authorDates: In print by 12 June 1965 · no author ever identified
answer.sourceLine: The six-or-eight pizza joke was already running as unsigned filler in American newspapers in June 1965, credited within months to several different tellers. The only documented link to George Carlin is a 1 November 1968 newspaper advertisement previewing Parade’s “Favorite Jokes of George Carlin” — which presents it as a joke he liked, three years after it was already in print.

source.excerpt: Ken Thompson stopped in at Dick McDaniels’ Pizza Palace the other night and ordered a pizza. When it was ready, Dick asked Ken if he wanted it cut in six or eight pieces. Ken thought a while, and then said, “Better make it six pieces. I could never eat eight.”
trail: 12 June 1965 — the joke appears as unsigned filler in the “Breezes” column of The News Herald (Franklin and Oil City, Pa.): a man in a local pizza shop, asked whether he wants six or eight pieces, thinks it over and picks six. This is the earliest instance documented by Barry Popik ↗.

20 September 1965 — Sports Illustrated prints the punchline as a real quotation from Milwaukee pitcher Dan Osinski: “Better make it six, I can’t eat eight.” The issue is readable in full at the Internet Archive ↗.

1 November 1968 — a newspaper advertisement previewing Parade’s “Favorite Jokes of George Carlin” runs the gag as a gem from Carlin’s favourites, per Quote Investigator ↗. That is the whole of the Carlin evidence.

24 November 1970 — the Fresno Bee quotes Mickey Mantle telling the story with Yogi Berra delivering the line, in a four-or-eight version; from here the joke belongs to Berra in popular memory (Barry Popik ↗).
source.excerptNote: The Weyauwega (Wis.) Chronicle item as reprinted in the Milwaukee Journal on 13 June 1965 (Barry Popik) and in the Omaha World Herald on 17 June 1965 — the latter the earliest instance Quote Investigator located. Note that “Do you want six or eight slices of pizza?” is the setup, not the punchline; the quotable half is the reply.

author.name: George Carlin
author.heading: Why Carlin gets the credit
author.metaLine: 1937–2008 · American comedian, satirist and social critic
author.bio: George Carlin was one of the most quoted comedians in America, and like Twain and Einstein before him he became a name that loose jokes drift toward. His one documented connection to this gag is a 1 November 1968 newspaper advertisement previewing Parade’s “Favorite Jokes of George Carlin,” which framed it as a joke he enjoyed — not one he wrote. By the time that ran, the same joke had been circulating in newspapers for three years, pinned to a Wisconsin pizza customer, a Milwaukee pitcher and several other people.

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been credited with it
misattribution.intro: This gag has been handed to at least half a dozen people in sixty years, and the documentary trail shows each of them receiving it rather than inventing it.

items.why: The only documented tie is a 1 November 1968 newspaper advertisement previewing Parade’s “Favorite Jokes of George Carlin,” which introduces it with “From the Favorite Jokes of George Carlin comes this gem” — a joke he liked, published three years after the joke was already in newspapers (Quote Investigator ↗).

Berra enters the story late. Mickey Mantle was quoted telling a Berra version in the Fresno Bee of 24 November 1970, and by then the joke had mutated from six-or-eight to four-or-eight (Barry Popik ↗).

items.why: Between June and November 1965 the identical gag was printed about a Wisconsin pizza customer, a New York Mets player, a stranger in a Chicago restaurant, a pitcher and a snack-bar patron in Bennett Cerf’s column — each presented as something that really happened (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: No one has been shown to have invented it. The earliest instances are unsigned newspaper filler from June 1965, and Quote Investigator’s own conclusion notes that some of these tellings “were constructed to entertain and were fictional” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A joke that goes looking for a famous mouth
lead: The line handed round as George Carlin’s is not really a quotation at all — it is a joke, and the wording “Do you want six or eight slices of pizza?” is the setup, the waitress’s question. The punchline is the answer: six, because I could never eat eight. In the earliest printings nobody famous says it. A man in a Pennsylvania pizza shop says it, overheard, in a column of local chatter on 12 June 1965.

What happened next is the standard life cycle of a good gag. Within five months of that first sighting it had been retold about a Wisconsin pizza customer, an unnamed New York Mets player, a stranger overheard in a Chicago restaurant, Milwaukee pitcher Dan Osinski and a snack-bar patron in Bennett Cerf’s syndicated column. Sports Illustrated printed it as a real quotation in September 1965. Carlin picked it up by 1968; by 1970 Mickey Mantle was telling it about Yogi Berra, and Berra has carried it ever since.
detailsBody: The joke needs a teller who is plausibly guileless, so it attaches to whoever currently plays that role in public. In 1965 that was a string of anonymous customers and journeyman ballplayers. Carlin, a rising comic building an act out of ordinary American absurdity, was a natural next stop. Berra, whose whole public persona was the deadpan logic-scrambler, was the final one — and the version that stuck to him swapped six-or-eight for four-or-eight.
Berra himself was blunt about this pattern. The line most often quoted back at him on the subject is his own: “I really didn’t say everything I said.”
context.pull: The joke did not come from a famous person. It went to them.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located citation is 17 June 1965 in an Omaha newspaper acknowledging the Weyauwega (Wis.) Chronicle: Ken Thompson at Dick McDaniels' Pizza Palace says "Better make it six pieces. I could never eat eight."

In 1968 Parade linked the joke to George Carlin: "From the Favorite Jokes of George Carlin comes this gem: A man ordering a pizza was asked if he wanted it sliced into six or eight pieces..."; QI's footnote cites a 1 November 1968 Augusta Chronicle advertisement previewing Parade.

The same 1965 joke was printed about Bobby Bragan's pitcher (LA Times, 23 July 1965), a diner overheard by Muriel Vernick (Chicago Tribune, 21 Aug 1965), Danny Osinski (via Joe Garagiola, 29 Oct 1965) and Andy Wimpfheimer (Bennett Cerf, 18 Nov 1965); QI concludes some tellings were fictional and that Yogi Berra was incorporated by the 1970s.

The earliest instance Barry Popik documents is 12 June 1965, The News Herald (Franklin and Oil City, PA), "Breezes," p. 7: "you better cut it into six pieces for I don't think I could eat eight!" — an anonymous man in a local pizza shop.
Popik records the Fresno Bee of 24 November 1970 quoting Mickey Mantle telling the joke about Yogi Berra in a four-or-eight version, and notes Berra is usually credited with the joke.

Sports Illustrated, 20 September 1965, "They Said It": Dan Osinski, Milwaukee pitcher, when a waitress asked if he wanted his pizza cut into six or eight pieces: "Better make it six, I can't eat eight."
George Carlin was born 12 May 1937 and died 22 June 2008; he is described as an American comedian, satirist, social critic, actor and author.
Yogi Berra (1925-2015) was often incorrectly credited with sayings he did not originate, and is quoted as saying "I really didn't say everything I said."
